subject: HSS
title: United States History and Geography: Making a New Nation
description: Fifth-grade U.S. history from the first peoples of North America through European exploration, the thirteen colonies, the American Revolution, the Constitution, and westward expansion to 1850. Following the 2016 CA HSS Framework, each unit is driven by an inquiry question and built on primary sources (journals, letters, maps, laws, engravings and speeches) read alongside multiple perspectives, including American Indian, African American and women's voices. A weekly map strand builds toward locating all 50 states and capitals.
framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards; 2016 California History–Social Science Framework

standards.5.1: Describe the major pre-Columbian settlements, including the cliff dwellers and pueblo people of the desert Southwest, the American Indians of the Pacific Northwest, the nomadic nations of the Great Plains, and the woodland peoples east of the Mississippi.
standards.5.1.1: Describe how geography and climate influenced the way various nations lived and adjusted to the natural environment, including locations of villages, structures, and use of resources.
standards.5.1.2: Describe their varied customs and folklore traditions.
standards.5.1.3: Explain their varied economies and systems of government.
standards.5.2: Trace the routes of early explorers and describe the early explorations of the Americas.
standards.5.2.1: Describe the entrepreneurial characteristics of early explorers and the technological developments (compass, astrolabe, seaworthy ships) that made sea exploration possible.
standards.5.2.2: Explain the aims, obstacles, and accomplishments of explorers, sponsors, and leaders of key European expeditions and the reasons Europeans chose to explore and colonize.
standards.5.2.3: Trace the routes of major land explorers of the United States and the Atlantic trade routes linking Africa, the West Indies, the British colonies, and Europe.
standards.5.2.4: Locate on maps of North and South America land claimed by Spain, France, England, Portugal, the Netherlands, Sweden, and Russia.
standards.5.3: Describe the cooperation and conflict that existed among the American Indians and between the Indian nations and the new settlers.
standards.5.3.1: Describe the competition among the English, French, Spanish, Dutch, and Indian nations for control of North America.
standards.5.3.2: Describe the cooperation between colonists and Indians during the 1600s and 1700s (agriculture, fur trade, military alliances, treaties, cultural interchanges).
standards.5.3.3: Examine the conflicts before the Revolutionary War (Pequot and King Philip's Wars, Powhatan Wars, French and Indian War).
standards.5.3.4: Discuss the role of broken treaties and massacres and the factors that led to Indians' defeat, including resistance to encroachment and assimilation.
standards.5.3.5: Describe the internecine Indian conflicts, including competing claims for control of lands.
standards.5.3.6: Explain the influence and achievements of significant leaders of the time (John Marshall, Andrew Jackson, Tecumseh, Chief Logan, John Ross, Sequoyah).
standards.5.4: Understand the political, religious, social, and economic institutions that evolved in the colonial era.
standards.5.4.1: Understand the influence of location and physical setting on the founding of the original 13 colonies and identify on a map the colonies and the American Indian nations already there.
standards.5.4.2: Identify the major individuals and groups responsible for founding the colonies and their reasons (John Smith, Roger Williams, William Penn, Lord Baltimore, William Bradford, John Winthrop).
standards.5.4.3: Describe the religious aspects of the earliest colonies (Puritanism, Anglicanism, Catholicism, Quakerism).
standards.5.4.4: Identify the significance and leaders of the First Great Awakening.
standards.5.4.5: Understand how the British colonial period created the basis for self-government and a free-market economy, and compare British, Spanish, and French colonial systems.
standards.5.4.6: Describe the introduction of slavery into America, the responses of enslaved families, the struggle between proponents and opponents of slavery, and its institutionalization in the South.
standards.5.4.7: Explain the early democratic ideas and practices of the colonial period, including representative assemblies and town meetings.
standards.5.5: Explain the causes of the American Revolution.
standards.5.5.1: Understand how political, religious, and economic ideas and interests brought about the Revolution (Stamp Act, Townshend Acts, taxes on tea, Coercive Acts).
standards.5.5.2: Know the significance of the First and Second Continental Congresses and the Committees of Correspondence.
standards.5.5.3: Understand the people and events associated with drafting and signing the Declaration of Independence and its key political concepts and significance.
standards.5.5.4: Describe the views, lives, and impact of key individuals (King George III, Patrick Henry, Thomas Jefferson, George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, John Adams).
standards.5.6: Understand the course and consequences of the American Revolution.
standards.5.6.1: Identify and map the major battles, campaigns, and turning points of the Revolutionary War, the roles of American and British leaders, and Indian alliances on both sides.
standards.5.6.2: Describe the contributions of France and other nations and individuals (Franklin, Lafayette, Kosciuszko, von Steuben) to the outcome of the Revolution.
standards.5.6.3: Identify the different roles women played during the Revolution (Abigail Adams, Martha Washington, Molly Pitcher, Phillis Wheatley, Mercy Otis Warren).
standards.5.6.4: Understand the personal impact and economic hardship on families caused by the war, including shortages and inflation.
standards.5.6.5: Explain how state constitutions established after 1776 embodied the ideals of the Revolution and served as models for the U.S. Constitution.
standards.5.6.6: Demonstrate knowledge of the land policies of the Continental Congress (Land Ordinance of 1785, Northwest Ordinance of 1787) and their impact on American Indians' land.
standards.5.6.7: Understand how the ideals of the Declaration of Independence changed the way people viewed slavery.
standards.5.7: Describe the people and events associated with the development of the U.S. Constitution and analyze its significance as the foundation of the American republic.
standards.5.7.1: List the shortcomings of the Articles of Confederation as set forth by their critics.
standards.5.7.2: Explain the significance of the Constitution of 1787, the struggles over its ratification, and the reasons for adding the Bill of Rights.
standards.5.7.3: Understand the fundamental principles of American constitutional democracy, including government power from the people and the primacy of individual liberty.
standards.5.7.4: Understand how the Constitution both empowers and limits the central government, and compare the powers of citizens, Congress, the president, the Supreme Court, and the states.
standards.5.7.5: Discuss the meaning of the American creed: safeguarding individual liberty within a unified nation, respecting the rule of law, and preserving the Constitution.
standards.5.7.6: Know the songs that express American ideals (e.g., 'America the Beautiful,' 'The Star-Spangled Banner').
standards.5.8: Trace the colonization, immigration, and settlement patterns of the American people from 1789 to the mid-1800s.
standards.5.8.1: Discuss the waves of immigrants from Europe between 1789 and 1850 and their modes of transportation (wagons, canals, flatboats, steamboats, Cumberland Gap).
standards.5.8.2: Name the states and territories that existed in 1850, their locations, and major geographical features.
standards.5.8.3: Demonstrate knowledge of the explorations of the trans-Mississippi West following the Louisiana Purchase (Lewis and Clark, Zebulon Pike, John Fremont).
standards.5.8.4: Discuss the experiences of settlers on the overland trails to the West, including the influence of terrain, rivers, vegetation, and climate.
standards.5.9: Know the location of the current 50 states and the names of their capitals.

units.title: Geography and the First Peoples of North America
units.big_idea: How did geography and climate shape the ways American Indian nations lived, governed and told their stories?

units.title: The Age of Exploration
units.big_idea: Why did Europeans explore, and what were the consequences of contact for the peoples of the Americas, Africa and Europe?

units.title: Founding the Thirteen Colonies
units.big_idea: Why did people come to the English colonies, and how did place shape colonial life?

units.title: Colonial Economy, Slavery and Self-Government
units.big_idea: How did colonial society plant seeds of both self-government and slavery?

units.title: Cooperation and Conflict in Colonial North America
units.big_idea: How did competition for land and trade lead to cooperation and conflict among colonists and Native nations?

units.title: The Road to Revolution
units.big_idea: Why would colonists break from the most powerful empire in the world?

units.title: The American Revolution
units.big_idea: How did the Patriots win independence, and did the Revolution's ideals apply to everyone?

units.title: Creating the Constitution
units.big_idea: How did the Constitution create a government that is both strong and limited?

units.title: A Growing Nation: Moving West
units.big_idea: How did westward expansion change the nation and the lives of American Indians and settlers?

units.title: States, Capitals and Year Review
units.big_idea: The nation that began as 13 colonies grew into 50 states.

weeks.topic: Geography of North America and map skills
objectives: Identify major landforms, regions and bodies of water of North America
Use latitude, longitude and map features
materials: blank outline maps of North America and the U.S.

days.title: Map skills
days.work: Review map parts (title, compass rose, scale, legend) and find 5 places using latitude and longitude on a world map.

days.title: Landforms
days.work: Label the Rocky Mountains, Appalachian Mountains, Great Plains, Mississippi River, Great Lakes and coasts on an outline map of North America.

days.title: Climate regions
days.work: Shade climate and vegetation regions (desert, forest, grassland, tundra) and write how each might affect how people live.

days.title: States strand: Northeast
days.work: Begin the 50-states strand by learning the 11 Northeast states and capitals with a blank map and flashcards.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a map quiz on North American landforms and Northeast states and capitals.

weeks.assessment: Map quiz on landforms, latitude/longitude and Northeast states.

weeks.topic: Peoples of the desert Southwest and Pacific Northwest
objectives: Explain how the Ancestral Pueblo and Pacific Northwest peoples adapted to their environments
Compare economies and customs
materials: photos of Mesa Verde and Taos Pueblo (NPS)
images of Kwakwaka'wakw or Tlingit art

days.title: Cliff dwellers
days.work: Explore NPS photos of Mesa Verde cliff dwellings and list how the people used the land, water and stone.

days.title: Pueblo life
days.work: Read about Pueblo farming of corn, beans and squash and build a model adobe dwelling from salt dough.

days.title: Pacific Northwest
days.work: Read about the Tlingit and Kwakwaka'wakw use of salmon and cedar and analyze a photo of a totem pole as a primary source.

days.title: Comparing regions
days.work: Complete a comparison chart of shelter, food, economy, government and customs for the two regions.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph explaining how environment shaped daily life in one region, using 3 details.

weeks.topic: Peoples of the Great Plains and the Eastern Woodlands
objectives: Explain how Plains nations relied on the bison
Describe the Haudenosaunee Confederacy's government
materials: excerpt of the Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace (NMAI Native Knowledge 360)

days.title: Plains nations
days.work: Read about the Lakota and other Plains nations and diagram the many uses of the bison.

days.title: Woodlands life
days.work: Read about Eastern Woodlands peoples (Haudenosaunee, Cherokee) and compare a longhouse to a tipi.

days.title: Primary source: Great Law of Peace
days.work: Analyze an excerpt of the Great Law of Peace and the Hiawatha wampum belt and explain how the five (later six) nations governed together.

days.title: Folklore
days.work: Read a Haudenosaunee or Lakota traditional story and identify what it teaches about values or nature.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on Plains and Woodlands peoples and explain one feature of Haudenosaunee government.

weeks.topic: Comparing First Peoples; unit project
objectives: Compare the four major regions of American Indian nations
Present findings about one nation
materials: research sources from NMAI Native Knowledge 360

days.title: Research
days.work: Choose one nation (e.g., Hopi, Chinook, Lakota, Cherokee) and research its homeland, food, shelter, government and stories.

days.title: Today's nations
days.work: Learn that these nations still exist today and find one fact about the nation's present-day government or culture.

days.title: Create the project
days.work: Create an illustrated poster or museum card set showing how geography shaped the nation's life.

days.title: States strand: Southeast
days.work: Learn Southeast states and capitals and locate the homelands of the Cherokee, Creek and Seminole on a map.

days.title: Unit 1 assessment
days.work: Present the project and take the Unit 1 test on First Peoples and Southeast states.

weeks.topic: Why explore? Motives and technology
objectives: Explain the reasons Europeans explored
Describe navigation technologies
materials: images of an astrolabe and caravel
cardboard, string and protractor to make an astrolabe

days.title: Gold, God and glory
days.work: Read about the reasons for European exploration (trade, wealth, religion, Reconquista, competition) and rank them with evidence.

days.title: Navigation tools
days.work: Build a simple astrolabe from cardboard and a protractor and measure the angle of a tall object.

days.title: Ships
days.work: Compare a caravel to earlier ships and explain how its design made long voyages possible.

days.title: Entrepreneurs
days.work: Analyze how explorers had to convince sponsors to fund voyages; write a short 'pitch' as an explorer.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on motives and navigation technology.

weeks.topic: Columbus and the Spanish in the Americas
objectives: Evaluate Columbus's voyages from multiple perspectives
Describe Spanish exploration of North America
materials: map of Coronado's and de Soto's routes

days.title: Primary source: Columbus's journal
days.work: Read the October 12, 1492 journal entry and note what Columbus observed and what he wanted.

days.title: Taíno perspective
days.work: Read about Taíno society and the effects of disease and forced labor after contact, and compare to Columbus's account.

days.title: Coronado and de Soto
days.work: Trace the routes of Coronado and de Soto on a map and record their goals, obstacles and results.

days.title: Columbian Exchange
days.work: Sort plants, animals and diseases that crossed the Atlantic in each direction and explain one lasting effect.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph evaluating Columbus's legacy from two perspectives.

weeks.topic: French, English and Dutch explorers
objectives: Trace routes of northern explorers searching for the Northwest Passage
Compare aims and accomplishments of explorers

days.title: John Cabot and Jacques Cartier
days.work: Trace Cabot's and Cartier's voyages and record their sponsors and findings.

days.title: Champlain and Hudson
days.work: Trace Champlain's and Hudson's routes and explain the search for the Northwest Passage.

days.title: Explorer comparison
days.work: Complete an explorer comparison matrix (sponsor, goal, obstacles, accomplishments) for 6 explorers.

days.title: Land claims map
days.work: Color a map showing land claimed by Spain, France, England, Portugal, the Netherlands, Sweden and Russia.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a map quiz on explorer routes and European land claims.

weeks.assessment: Explorer matrix and land claims map quiz.

weeks.topic: The Atlantic world and unit review
objectives: Trace Atlantic trade routes linking Africa, the West Indies, the colonies and Europe
Summarize the impact of exploration

days.title: Atlantic trade routes
days.work: Draw the Atlantic trade routes and label goods carried on each leg.

days.title: The Middle Passage
days.work: Read an age-appropriate excerpt from Olaudah Equiano's narrative (1789) and discuss what it reveals about the Middle Passage.

days.title: States strand: Midwest
days.work: Learn the 12 Midwest states and capitals with a blank map and flashcards.

days.title: Unit review
days.work: Create a timeline of key explorations from 1492 to 1610 and review vocabulary.

days.title: Unit 2 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 2 test on exploration and the Midwest states.

weeks.topic: Jamestown and the Virginia Colony
objectives: Explain why Jamestown was founded and why it struggled
Describe relations with the Powhatan Confederacy
materials: John Smith's 1612 map of Virginia (Library of Congress)

days.title: Founding Jamestown
days.work: Read about the Virginia Company's goals and the 1607 founding and list the problems settlers faced.

days.title: Primary source: John Smith's map
days.work: Analyze John Smith's 1612 map of Virginia, noting Powhatan towns and what the map reveals about the land.

days.title: Powhatan and Pocahontas
days.work: Read about the Powhatan Confederacy and the real Pocahontas and separate fact from legend.

days.title: Tobacco and Anglicanism
days.work: Explain how tobacco saved the colony and describe the role of the Anglican Church in Virginia.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a cause-and-effect chart of Jamestown's struggles and successes.

weeks.assessment: Map analysis sheet and cause-effect chart.

weeks.topic: Plymouth and the Massachusetts Bay Colony
objectives: Analyze the Mayflower Compact as an early form of self-government
Describe Puritan beliefs and life
materials: excerpt of William Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation

days.title: Pilgrims and Wampanoag
days.work: Read about the Pilgrims' voyage and the Wampanoag people, including Massasoit and Tisquantum (Squanto).

days.title: Primary source: Mayflower Compact
days.work: Read the Mayflower Compact, paraphrase it, and explain why it matters to self-government.

days.title: Bradford's account
days.work: Read an excerpt of Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation on the first winter and the 1621 harvest and compare it to a Wampanoag perspective.

days.title: Puritans
days.work: Read about John Winthrop's 'city upon a hill' and Puritan life and write what Puritans valued.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on the New England founding and write a two-sentence summary of the Mayflower Compact.

weeks.topic: New England colonies and religious dissent
objectives: Explain why Rhode Island and Connecticut were founded
Describe New England geography and economy

days.title: Roger Williams
days.work: Read about Roger Williams's banishment and the founding of Rhode Island on ideas of religious freedom.

days.title: Anne Hutchinson and Thomas Hooker
days.work: Compare Anne Hutchinson's and Thomas Hooker's disagreements with Puritan leaders.

days.title: Geography and economy
days.work: Map New England's rocky soil, forests and harbors and explain how they led to fishing, shipbuilding and trade.

days.title: Colonial diary
days.work: Write a diary entry as a child in a New England town, using 5 accurate details.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Label the New England colonies and take a quiz on their founders and reasons.

weeks.topic: Middle and Southern colonies
objectives: Identify founders and reasons for the Middle and Southern colonies
Compare regional economies
materials: William Penn's 1681 charter or letter excerpt

days.title: Pennsylvania
days.work: Read about William Penn and the Quakers and analyze an excerpt of Penn's letter to the Lenape about fair dealings.

days.title: New York, New Jersey, Delaware
days.work: Learn how New Netherland became New York and why the Middle Colonies were diverse 'breadbasket' colonies.

days.title: Maryland and the South
days.work: Read about Lord Baltimore's Catholic haven in Maryland and the founding of the Carolinas and Georgia.

days.title: Regions chart
days.work: Complete a 3-region chart comparing geography, economy, religion and founders of the colonies.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Label all 13 colonies and take a quiz on Middle and Southern colony founders.

weeks.topic: The First Great Awakening and colonial daily life
objectives: Explain the significance of the Great Awakening
Describe daily life, work and education in the colonies
materials: excerpt describing George Whitefield's preaching (Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography)

days.title: Great Awakening
days.work: Read about Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield and Franklin's account of hearing Whitefield preach; explain how revivals encouraged questioning authority.

days.title: Colonial work
days.work: Read about apprentices and artisans (blacksmith, cooper, printer) and choose a trade to research.

days.title: Hands-on colonial life
days.work: Try a colonial craft or chore (dipping a candle with adult help, making butter in a jar, writing with a quill).

days.title: States strand: South
days.work: Review Southeast states and learn the South Central states and capitals (TX, OK, AR, LA).

days.title: Unit 3 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 3 test on founding the colonies and colonial life.

weeks.topic: Colonial economy and the British system
objectives: Explain how the colonial economy worked
Compare British, Spanish and French colonial systems

days.title: Mercantilism
days.work: Play a simple trade simulation showing raw materials going to England and finished goods returning, then discuss who benefits.

days.title: Free enterprise roots
days.work: Read how colonists ran farms, shops and ships for profit and explain the start of a free-market economy.

days.title: Spanish and French colonies
days.work: Read about Spanish missions and presidios (including California) and French fur-trading posts.

days.title: Comparing systems
days.work: Complete a chart comparing British, Spanish and French colonies in government, economy, religion and relations with Native peoples.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph explaining one major difference between British and Spanish colonies.

weeks.topic: Slavery in the colonies
objectives: Describe the introduction and growth of slavery
Explain how enslaved people resisted and preserved their culture
materials: Phillis Wheatley poem 'On Being Brought from Africa to America'

days.title: 1619 and beyond
days.work: Read about the arrival of enslaved Africans in Virginia in 1619 and how slavery became law over the following decades.

days.title: Lives of enslaved families
days.work: Read about enslaved families' work, culture, music and faith and how they kept traditions alive.

days.title: Resistance
days.work: Learn about forms of resistance including slowdowns, escape and the Stono Rebellion, and record examples.

days.title: Opposing slavery
days.work: Analyze the 1688 Germantown Quaker Petition and Phillis Wheatley's poem as early voices in the debate.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph explaining how slavery became institutionalized in the South, using two sources.

weeks.topic: Seeds of self-government
objectives: Explain representative assemblies and town meetings
Connect colonial practices to democracy

days.title: Rights of Englishmen
days.work: Read about the Magna Carta and English Bill of Rights and list rights colonists expected.

days.title: House of Burgesses
days.work: Learn how the House of Burgesses (1619) worked and who could vote.

days.title: Town meeting
days.work: Hold a family town meeting on a real household decision, using majority vote and taking minutes.

days.title: Who was left out?
days.work: Discuss who could and could not vote in colonial assemblies (women, enslaved people, Native Americans, non-landowners).

days.title: Unit 4 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 4 test on colonial economy, slavery and self-government.

weeks.assessment: Town meeting minutes and Unit 4 test.

weeks.topic: Cooperation: trade, alliances and exchange
objectives: Describe cooperation between colonists and Native nations
Explain the fur trade and alliances
materials: Penn's Treaty with the Lenape painting (Benjamin West, 1771)

days.title: Agriculture and survival
days.work: Read about how Native peoples taught colonists to grow corn and use local resources.

days.title: The fur trade
days.work: Map the French and Dutch fur trade networks and explain what each side gained.

days.title: Primary source: painting
days.work: Analyze Benjamin West's painting of Penn's treaty and discuss how a painting made 90 years later can shape memory.

days.title: Cultural exchange
days.work: List words, foods and technologies exchanged between Native nations and colonists.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a summary of three forms of cooperation with examples.

weeks.topic: Conflict: Powhatan Wars, Pequot War and King Philip's War
objectives: Explain causes and effects of early colonial wars
Analyze broken treaties and their consequences
materials: excerpt of Mary Rowlandson's narrative or Metacom's 1675 grievances

days.title: Powhatan Wars
days.work: Read about the Powhatan Wars in Virginia and list causes, including land and tobacco expansion.

days.title: Pequot War
days.work: Read about the Pequot War and the Mystic massacre and discuss how colonists and Native allies fought.

days.title: King Philip's War
days.work: Read Metacom's reported grievances (1675) and explain why he resisted colonial expansion.

days.title: Native rivalries
days.work: Read about rivalries among Native nations (Haudenosaunee and Huron) and how Europeans used them.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Create a cause-and-effect timeline of the colonial wars and take a quiz.

weeks.topic: The French and Indian War
objectives: Explain the causes, alliances and outcome of the French and Indian War
Connect the war's debt to future conflict with Britain

days.title: Competition for the Ohio Valley
days.work: Map British, French and Native claims to the Ohio Valley and explain why war began in 1754.

days.title: Primary source: 'Join, or Die'
days.work: Analyze Franklin's 'Join, or Die' cartoon and explain its message about colonial unity.

days.title: Alliances and outcome
days.work: Chart which Native nations allied with France or Britain and compare 1754 and 1763 maps.

days.title: Pontiac and the Proclamation
days.work: Read about Pontiac's resistance and the Proclamation of 1763 and explain why colonists were angry.

days.title: Unit 5 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 5 test on cooperation and conflict and review West states and capitals.

weeks.topic: Taxation without representation
objectives: Explain British tax policies after 1763
Describe colonial resistance
materials: Stamp Act protest broadside (Library of Congress)

days.title: Britain's debt
days.work: Role-play Parliament and colonists debating who should pay for the French and Indian War.

days.title: Stamp Act
days.work: Examine an image of a tax stamp and a protest broadside and list items that were taxed.

days.title: Resistance
days.work: Read about the Stamp Act Congress, boycotts and the Sons and Daughters of Liberty.

days.title: Townshend Acts
days.work: Explain the Townshend Acts and the boycott of British goods; calculate the cost of taxed items in a simple chart.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a letter as a colonist to Parliament protesting the taxes using 'no taxation without representation.'

weeks.topic: Boston Massacre, Boston Tea Party and the Coercive Acts
objectives: Analyze Paul Revere's engraving as propaganda
Explain how the Tea Party led to the Coercive Acts

days.title: Boston Massacre engraving
days.work: Analyze Paul Revere's engraving, listing details that make the British look guilty.

days.title: Another account
days.work: Compare the engraving with Captain Preston's account and decide why the stories differ.

days.title: Boston Tea Party
days.work: Read about the Tea Act and Tea Party and write a newspaper headline from both Patriot and Loyalist views.

days.title: Coercive Acts and Committees
days.work: List the Coercive Acts and explain how Committees of Correspondence helped colonies unite.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz and create a cause-and-effect chain from the Stamp Act to the Coercive Acts.

weeks.topic: The Continental Congresses and the first shots
objectives: Explain the significance of the First and Second Continental Congresses
Describe Lexington and Concord
materials: Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty' speech excerpt (1775)

days.title: First Continental Congress
days.work: Read about the 1774 Congress and list its decisions.

days.title: Patrick Henry
days.work: Read and perform an excerpt of Patrick Henry's 1775 speech and explain its argument.

days.title: Lexington and Concord
days.work: Map Revere's and Dawes's rides and the battles at Lexington and Concord.

days.title: Second Continental Congress
days.work: Explain how the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army and chose Washington.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a Patriot vs. Loyalist T-chart of beliefs and take a quiz.

weeks.topic: Common Sense and the Declaration of Independence
objectives: Analyze key ideas in the Declaration
Describe the people who drafted and signed it
materials: excerpt of Thomas Paine's Common Sense

days.title: Common Sense
days.work: Read a short excerpt of Common Sense and explain how Paine persuaded ordinary colonists.

days.title: Drafting the Declaration
days.work: Learn about the Committee of Five (Jefferson, Adams, Franklin, Sherman, Livingston) and how the Declaration was written.

days.title: The Preamble
days.work: Paraphrase the Declaration's second paragraph and explain unalienable rights and consent of the governed.

days.title: Grievances
days.work: Match 5 grievances against King George III to events studied earlier.

days.title: Unit 6 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 6 test on the causes of the Revolution and the Declaration.

weeks.topic: Early battles and turning points
objectives: Map major battles and campaigns
Explain why Saratoga was a turning point

days.title: Strengths and weaknesses
days.work: Compare the strengths and weaknesses of the British and Continental armies in a chart.

days.title: Bunker Hill to Trenton
days.work: Map Bunker Hill, the loss of New York and Washington's crossing to Trenton.

days.title: Saratoga
days.work: Read about Saratoga and explain why it convinced France to join the war.

days.title: Valley Forge
days.work: Read an excerpt of Washington's letter describing Valley Forge hardships and list soldiers' needs.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Create an annotated battle map with 5 battles and their significance.

weeks.topic: Allies, heroes and Native nations in the war
objectives: Describe foreign contributions to victory
Explain Native alliances on both sides
materials: map of Spanish campaigns on the Gulf Coast

days.title: France joins
days.work: Read about Franklin's negotiations in Paris and the French alliance of 1778.

days.title: Foreign heroes
days.work: Create biography cards for Lafayette, von Steuben, Kosciuszko and Bernardo de Gálvez.

days.title: Native alliances
days.work: Read about the Oneida who supported the Patriots and Joseph Brant (Mohawk) who supported the British, and explain each nation's reasons.

days.title: African American soldiers
days.work: Read about the 1st Rhode Island Regiment and Lord Dunmore's Proclamation and explain why Black Americans fought on both sides.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on allies and individuals who shaped the war.

weeks.topic: Women, families and the home front
objectives: Identify roles women played
Describe wartime hardships

days.title: Remember the Ladies
days.work: Read Abigail Adams's 1776 letter and John's reply and discuss what she asked for.

days.title: Women in the war
days.work: Research Martha Washington, Molly Pitcher, Phillis Wheatley and Mercy Otis Warren and create a 'women of the Revolution' chart.

days.title: Inflation
days.work: Use a simple price table to model how Continental dollars lost value ('not worth a Continental').

days.title: Freedom for whom?
days.work: Read about Elizabeth Freeman (Mum Bett) suing for freedom in Massachusetts and discuss how Declaration ideals changed views on slavery.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a letter as a family member on the home front describing hardships with accurate details.

weeks.topic: Victory at Yorktown and new governments
objectives: Explain how the war ended
Describe state constitutions and land ordinances

days.title: Yorktown
days.work: Map the Yorktown campaign showing the French fleet and armies trapping Cornwallis.

days.title: Treaty of Paris 1783
days.work: Compare maps before and after the Treaty of Paris and list the treaty's terms.

days.title: State constitutions
days.work: Read excerpts of the 1780 Massachusetts Constitution and identify ideas taken from the Declaration.

days.title: Land ordinances
days.work: Draw a township grid from the Land Ordinance of 1785 and read how the Northwest Ordinance banned slavery yet took Native lands.

days.title: Unit 7 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 7 test on the course and consequences of the Revolution.

weeks.topic: The Articles of Confederation
objectives: List weaknesses of the Articles
Explain Shays' Rebellion

days.title: A weak union
days.work: Read about the Articles of Confederation and list 5 powers Congress did and did not have.

days.title: Simulation
days.work: Play a simulation where each 'state' prints its own money and taxes trade, then discuss problems.

days.title: Shays' Rebellion
days.work: Read about Shays' Rebellion and explain why it alarmed leaders like Washington.

days.title: Critics' views
days.work: Read quotes from critics of the Articles and match each to a weakness.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph explaining why leaders called the Constitutional Convention.

weeks.topic: The Constitutional Convention
objectives: Describe the compromises of the Convention
Analyze the Preamble

days.title: Philadelphia 1787
days.work: Read about the delegates and James Madison's role and list who was not represented.

days.title: Great Compromise
days.work: Compare the Virginia and New Jersey Plans and explain the Great Compromise with a diagram.

days.title: Slavery and the Constitution
days.work: Read about the Three-Fifths Compromise and the slave trade clause and discuss why they were controversial.

days.title: Primary source: Preamble
days.work: Paraphrase each phrase of the Preamble and illustrate one goal.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Recite the Preamble and take a quiz on the Convention's compromises.

weeks.topic: Three branches, checks and balances, and federalism
objectives: Explain the three branches and their powers
Compare federal and state powers

days.title: Legislative branch
days.work: Read Article I basics and diagram how a bill becomes a law.

days.title: Executive and judicial
days.work: Read about the president's and Supreme Court's powers and complete a three-branch tree.

days.title: Checks and balances
days.work: Play an iCivics checks-and-balances game and list 4 checks between branches.

days.title: Federalism
days.work: Sort 15 powers into federal, state or shared (e.g., printing money, schools, taxes).

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on branches, checks and balances and federalism.

weeks.topic: Ratification, the Bill of Rights and the American creed
objectives: Explain the ratification debate and Bill of Rights
Discuss the American creed and patriotic songs
materials: lyrics of 'The Star-Spangled Banner' and 'America the Beautiful'

days.title: Ratification debate
days.work: Role-play a debate between a Federalist and an Anti-Federalist about ratifying the Constitution.

days.title: Bill of Rights
days.work: Paraphrase the first 10 amendments and create an illustrated Bill of Rights booklet.

days.title: Rights in action
days.work: Read 6 scenarios and decide which amendment protects the person in each.

days.title: American creed and songs
days.work: Read and sing 'The Star-Spangled Banner' and 'America the Beautiful' and explain which ideals each expresses.

days.title: Unit 8 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 8 test on the Constitution and Bill of Rights.

weeks.assessment: Bill of Rights booklet and Unit 8 test.

weeks.topic: Crossing the Appalachians and new immigrants
objectives: Describe routes and transportation west
Discuss immigration waves 1789–1850
materials: Erie Canal song lyrics ('Low Bridge, Everybody Down')

days.title: Daniel Boone and the Cumberland Gap
days.work: Trace the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap and explain why it mattered.

days.title: Canals and steamboats
days.work: Compare travel times by wagon, flatboat, canal and steamboat and sing the Erie Canal song.

days.title: Immigrants
days.work: Read about German and Irish immigrants before 1850 and why they came.

days.title: 1850 map
days.work: Label the states and territories of 1850 and major rivers and mountain ranges.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on transportation and the 1850 map.

weeks.topic: The Louisiana Purchase and western explorers
objectives: Explain the Louisiana Purchase
Trace the journeys of Lewis and Clark, Pike and Frémont
materials: excerpts from the Lewis and Clark journals (Library of Congress)

days.title: Louisiana Purchase
days.work: Read about Jefferson's 1803 purchase and calculate its size compared to the existing U.S.

days.title: Lewis and Clark journals
days.work: Read journal excerpts describing animals and landscapes and sketch one like a naturalist.

days.title: Sacagawea and York
days.work: Research the contributions of Sacagawea and York to the expedition.

days.title: Pike and Frémont
days.work: Trace Pike's and Frémont's routes and record what each found, including Frémont in California.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a journal entry as a member of the Corps of Discovery with accurate geography.

weeks.topic: Native nations and removal
objectives: Explain leaders and resistance of Native nations
Describe the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears
materials: excerpt of John Ross's 1836 letter to Congress

days.title: Tecumseh
days.work: Read about Tecumseh's confederacy and an excerpt of his speech urging unity, and explain his goals.

days.title: Sequoyah
days.work: Examine the Cherokee syllabary and explain how Sequoyah's invention and the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper strengthened the nation.

days.title: Marshall vs. Jackson
days.work: Learn about Worcester v. Georgia (John Marshall) and Andrew Jackson's refusal to enforce it.

days.title: Trail of Tears
days.work: Read John Ross's 1836 letter to Congress and a map of removal routes; discuss the human cost.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph on how one leader responded to the loss of Native lands, using a primary source.

weeks.topic: The overland trails
objectives: Describe settlers' experiences on the Oregon, California and Santa Fe Trails
Explain how geography affected the journey
materials: masking tape to outline a wagon (4 x 10 ft)

days.title: Trails map
days.work: Map the Oregon, California, Mormon and Santa Fe Trails and label rivers, mountains and landmarks like Chimney Rock.

days.title: Packing the wagon
days.work: Tape a 4-by-10-foot wagon outline on the floor and choose supplies that fit, explaining each choice.

days.title: Pioneer diaries
days.work: Read excerpts of pioneer women's diaries and list hardships caused by terrain, rivers and climate.

days.title: Arrival in California
days.work: Read about the Donner Party crossing the Sierra Nevada and life at the end of the California Trail.

days.title: Unit 9 assessment
days.work: Take the Unit 9 test on westward movement.

weeks.topic: 50 states and capitals; year review
objectives: Locate all 50 states and name their capitals
Connect the year's inquiry questions

days.title: Western states
days.work: Learn the remaining Mountain and Pacific states and capitals, including Alaska and Hawaii.

days.title: All 50 practice
days.work: Practice all 50 states and capitals with a blank map game and online puzzle.

days.title: Timeline review
days.work: Build a class timeline from first peoples to 1850 with 20 key events from the year.

days.title: Being a citizen
days.work: Write a reflection on the American creed: one right you value and one responsibility you will practice.

days.title: Final assessment
days.work: Take the 50 states and capitals map test and a year-end history review.

weeks.assessment: 50 states and capitals test and year-end review.
